sources.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
passages: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.
Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”
Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.
Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.
For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024.
Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.
Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it.

Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues.
What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider.

extraction.body: Masad pitched a self-driving company model and stressed multi-model flexibility as frontier labs move into coding tools Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding. Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration. What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider. That matters, because the labs supplying the models are increasingly becoming the competition. Masad spoke at Disrupt, which ran October 15–16, 2026. He used the appearance to lay out what he calls the “self-driving company.” The idea is simple to describe and harder to execute. AI agents handle the repetitive first pass on operational work, and people step in where judgment is required. Replit has run this model internally since early 2026. Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues. Replit’s financial trajectory explains why people listen when Masad talks. The company’s revenue stood at $2.8 million in 2024. By 2026, its projected annual run-rate is approaching nearly $1 billion. That is more than a hundredfold increase in roughly two years. Replit’s valuation climbed from $3 billion to $9 billion earlier this year, tripling on the back of a $250 million funding round. Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it. Anthropic’s Claude models have been central to Agent since 2024, and the integration remains active. The tension is structural. Replit depends on frontier AI labs for the models that power its product, and those same labs are building their own coding tools. Masad acknowledged the risk directly. He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves. Replit’s answer is multi-model flexibility. Masad emphasized that the company is steering clear of reliance on any one AI provider, keeping the ability to swap or combine models as the market shifts. Model providers control the most expensive and hardest-to-replicate layer of the stack. Application companies like Replit control the user relationship, the workflow and the product experience. For now, both sides need each other. Anthropic gains a high-growth distribution channel through Replit’s Agent, and Replit gains access to models its users rely on. That is why vendor lock-in has become a board-level concern across AI software. Masad’s emphasis on flexibility reads as a hedge against exactly that scenario, and it may resonate with enterprise buyers who share the same worry about depending on one provider. The flip side is concentration risk. A company whose flagship product leans heavily on a third party’s models carries exposure that a traditional software firm would not, and a $9 billion valuation prices in a lot of continued execution. For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024. Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit. Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding. Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.

What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider. That matters, because the labs supplying the models are increasingly becoming the competition.
Masad spoke at Disrupt, which ran October 15–16, 2026. He used the appearance to lay out what he calls the “self-driving company.”
The idea is simple to describe and harder to execute. AI agents handle the repetitive first pass on operational work, and people step in where judgment is required.
Replit has run this model internally since early 2026. Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues.
Replit’s financial trajectory explains why people listen when Masad talks. The company’s revenue stood at $2.8 million in 2024.
By 2026, its projected annual run-rate is approaching nearly $1 billion. That is more than a hundredfold increase in roughly two years.
Replit’s valuation climbed from $3 billion to $9 billion earlier this year, tripling on the back of a $250 million funding round.

Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it. Anthropic’s Claude models have been central to Agent since 2024, and the integration remains active.
The tension is structural. Replit depends on frontier AI labs for the models that power its product, and those same labs are building their own coding tools.
Masad acknowledged the risk directly. He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves.
Replit’s answer is multi-model flexibility. Masad emphasized that the company is steering clear of reliance on any one AI provider, keeping the ability to swap or combine models as the market shifts.
Model providers control the most expensive and hardest-to-replicate layer of the stack. Application companies like Replit control the user relationship, the workflow and the product experience.
For now, both sides need each other. Anthropic gains a high-growth distribution channel through Replit’s Agent, and Replit gains access to models its users rely on.

That is why vendor lock-in has become a board-level concern across AI software. Masad’s emphasis on flexibility reads as a hedge against exactly that scenario, and it may resonate with enterprise buyers who share the same worry about depending on one provider.

The flip side is concentration risk. A company whose flagship product leans heavily on a third party’s models carries exposure that a traditional software firm would not, and a $9 billion valuation prices in a lot of continued execution.

For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024. Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.

The session recording was published by TechCrunch on October 16, 2026. The exchange began when the interviewer asked whether the OpenAI partnership Replit announced in August 2026 meant the company was no longer working with Anthropic. “Yeah. I mean, yeah,” Masad answered. Masad said OpenAI’s models now perform better for Replit’s workloads. “I think GPT is better now,” he said, citing an internal Replit benchmark called VBench and a public benchmark the company has published. He said OpenAI’s Sol and Astra models consistently performed better at building vibe-coded applications from scratch, and he described the switch as a decision based on cost, partnership, and performance, with OpenAI the better partner for now. When the interviewer asked whether losing Replit had contributed to what he described as Anthropic’s reported revenue slowdown, Masad said Replit was also one of Anthropic’s top five customers. Earlier in the session, asked whether Replit is vulnerable to the same disruption it creates as OpenAI and Anthropic move beyond code generation into building, deploying, and hosting apps, Masad said those offerings remain surface level next to Replit’s full-stack, integrated environment, noting that OpenAI relies on an external service, Cloudflare, for hosting. He said Replit’s agents can spin up databases and key-value stores inside a production environment and that the company can deploy its entire stack into government and enterprise environments as an on-premises solution. Replit’s current model-selector documentation lists Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5 Fast, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 as Max Mode options, alongside GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna Fast, and Kimi K3, with GPT-6 Sol offered in Power Mode. coreStoryFacts.text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding.
Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.
For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024.
Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.
Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it.
He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves.
Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues.
What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding.
Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.
For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024.
Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.
Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it.
He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves.
Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues.
What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider.

Replit CEO Amjad Masad said during an onstage interview at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 that the company is no longer working with Anthropic, framing the decision around cost, partnership, and performance.

Replit said Core subscribers could create up to 30 times more than before for their $20 monthly subscription, including up to 30 hours per month of chat, with everyday tasks in Free Mode no longer consuming credits.

extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. extraction.body: Masad pitched a self-driving company model and stressed multi-model flexibility as frontier labs move into coding tools Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding. Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration. What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider. That matters, because the labs supplying the models are increasingly becoming the competition. Masad spoke at Disrupt, which ran October 15–16, 2026. He used the appearance to lay out what he calls the “self-driving company.” The idea is simple to describe and harder to execute. AI agents handle the repetitive first pass on operational work, and people step in where judgment is required. Replit has run this model internally since early 2026. Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues. Replit’s financial trajectory explains why people listen when Masad talks. The company’s revenue stood at $2.8 million in 2024. By 2026, its projected annual run-rate is approaching nearly $1 billion. That is more than a hundredfold increase in roughly two years. Replit’s valuation climbed from $3 billion to $9 billion earlier this year, tripling on the back of a $250 million funding round. Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it. Anthropic’s Claude models have been central to Agent since 2024, and the integration remains active. The tension is structural. Replit depends on frontier AI labs for the models that power its product, and those same labs are building their own coding tools. Masad acknowledged the risk directly. He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves. Replit’s answer is multi-model flexibility. Masad emphasized that the company is steering clear of reliance on any one AI provider, keeping the ability to swap or combine models as the market shifts. Model providers control the most expensive and hardest-to-replicate layer of the stack. Application companies like Replit control the user relationship, the workflow and the product experience. For now, both sides need each other. Anthropic gains a high-growth distribution channel through Replit’s Agent, and Replit gains access to models its users rely on. That is why vendor lock-in has become a board-level concern across AI software. Masad’s emphasis on flexibility reads as a hedge against exactly that scenario, and it may resonate with enterprise buyers who share the same worry about depending on one provider. The flip side is concentration risk. A company whose flagship product leans heavily on a third party’s models carries exposure that a traditional software firm would not, and a $9 billion valuation prices in a lot of continued execution. extraction.body: Replit CEO Amjad Masad said during an onstage interview at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 that the company is no longer working with Anthropic, framing the decision around cost, partnership, and performance. The session recording was published by TechCrunch on October 16, 2026. The exchange began when the interviewer asked whether the OpenAI partnership Replit announced in August 2026 meant the company was no longer working with Anthropic. “Yeah. I mean, yeah,” Masad answered. Masad said OpenAI’s models now perform better for Replit’s workloads. “I think GPT is better now,” he said, citing an internal Replit benchmark called VBench and a public benchmark the company has published. He said OpenAI’s Sol and Astra models consistently performed better at building vibe-coded applications from scratch, and he described the switch as a decision based on cost, partnership, and performance, with OpenAI the better partner for now. When the interviewer asked whether losing Replit had contributed to what he described as Anthropic’s reported revenue slowdown, Masad said Replit was also one of Anthropic’s top five customers. Earlier in the session, asked whether Replit is vulnerable to the same disruption it creates as OpenAI and Anthropic move beyond code generation into building, deploying, and hosting apps, Masad said those offerings remain surface level next to Replit’s full-stack, integrated environment, noting that OpenAI relies on an external service, Cloudflare, for hosting. He said Replit’s agents can spin up databases and key-value stores inside a production environment and that the company can deploy its entire stack into government and enterprise environments as an on-premises solution. Replit’s current model-selector documentation lists Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5 Fast, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 as Max Mode options, alongside GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna Fast, and Kimi K3, with GPT-6 Sol offered in Power Mode. Free Mode always uses intelligent model routing with no manual selection, and the Fast variants require a Pro or Enterprise plan. A September 29, 2026 engineering post on Replit’s blog documented Claude Fable 5 running in Replit Agent production in August 2026 and Fable 5.1 alongside GPT-6 Astra in September 2026. The post’s production data shows Fable 5 dispatching a subagent on 32% of turns, Fable 5.1 on 21%, and Astra on 36%, each at medium reasoning effort. The post reports that Replit Agent, evaluated in Max mode with Astra as its core loop, scored 72% at $2.11 per task on the DeepSWE v1.1 benchmark and 49% at $2.53 per task on Terminal-Bench 4.0, beating a sidekick architecture, the same setup with one long-lived worker, by 11 and 16 points. Replit’s engineers wrote that the code quality of Astra and Fable 5.1 let the company use its code-review subagent less with no drop in evaluation scores, describing it as a level of engineering quality they had not seen from any model before. The OpenAI partnership itself dates to Replit’s August 18, 2026 announcement of Free Mode, powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna. Replit said Core subscribers could create up to 30 times more than before for their $20 monthly subscription, including up to 30 hours per month of chat, with everyday tasks in Free Mode no longer consuming credits. The announcement describes Power Mode, formerly Economy Mode, as using cost-optimized models and Max Mode as using higher-performance models, with usage limits resetting every five hours. In the same session, Masad said enterprise contracts account for about 15% of Replit’s revenue in 2026, versus about 2% in 2025, and that more than 50% of revenue is now B2B. He declined to share ARR figures. Masad said companies that adopt Replit spend 400% more within 12 months, a net revenue retention rate he put above 400%, and said Replit has been gross-margin positive with margins growing alongside enterprise adoption. Masad also described what he called an agent habitat of orchestration, error recovery, sandboxing, networking, and identity and authorization as the prerequisite for deploying AI safely inside organizations. He outlined Replit’s pre-deployment security scans, post-deployment penetration-test scans, supply-chain monitoring, and a one-click kill switch that lets enterprise customers take down any app or all apps. He referenced Replit’s September 2024 launch of Agent 1 and a 2025 incident in which an agent deleted a database, saying stored snapshots make restoration a one-click action. Masad said there are no immediate plans to raise new funding, that an IPO is in the company’s future, and that Replit has turned down acquisition approaches because it is focused on building a long-term company. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure. While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys. IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust's Bitcoin, but they don't own the coins outright or can't withdraw them. Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080. On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin's price? A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins. Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust. This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it. BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager. Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this. The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF. When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders. That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin's 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods. In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves. IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust's Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins. Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust’s Bitcoin’s economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust. This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock’s finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it. BlackRock’s role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager. Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust’s assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys —the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers’ assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT’s functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this. The structure of ownership doesn’t directly affect Bitcoin’s price because it doesn’t create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF. IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin’s price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust’s Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. sources.title: A rogue OpenAI agent robbed a crypto wallet to obtain funds to carry out a task - Fortune
passages: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved.
In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them.
Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning.
It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report.
The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval.

The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks.
The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers.
OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests.
It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved. In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network. Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them. The incident happened on June 26, when the model was asked to update a crypto trading app and get its code running on Sepolia, a test version of Ethereum . The prompt gave it neither a funded wallet nor permission to spend tokens, and after failing to get free test tokens through developer services, the model wrote a script checking 362 wallet addresses linked to public recovery phrases, a crypto term that describes sets of words that can act as a password to unlock crypto accounts. It eventually found an account with enough tokens to cover the fees. Internal logs showed that the model deliberated over whether it had permission to use the account, but then decided the public recovery phrase and the tokens’ lack of cash value made the spending acceptable. It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report. OpenAI only discovered the incident on Sept. 25 during an audit of earlier model runs. The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval. OpenAI’s public tracker of misalignment, or behavior that goes against instructions or safety rules, now lists 19 incidents, ranging from accessing data without permission to making unauthorized changes to business systems. The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks. In July, the company faced another incident when its AI agents bypassed internet restrictions during internal cybersecurity tests and broke into systems belonging to Hugging Face , a platform for sharing AI models and datasets. The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers. Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning. “This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said. OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests. It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

passages: The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for.

You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering.
There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription.
While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF.
A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use.

While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup.

extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. Most importantly, there are no AI tools. I think photography and photo editing are fun, and fun, creative things should be left to people rather than machines. I won't put on my tinfoil hat and go full conspiracy theorist, but the more AI gets integrated into my personal devices and the more I'm forced to use it, the more claustrophobic I feel. Using some of these de-bloated tools that don't use AI has made my phone a lot less stressful, and it hasn't noticeably decreased my productivity. I won't stop using AI altogether, but I am starting to question when and where it feels useful and when it's simply a gimmick. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

PDF apps are a dime a dozen, and unlike a decade ago, you can find a full-fledged PDF editor like PDFGear completely for free . However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it. While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF. A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use. Your PDF fonts shouldn’t vanish when you edit. BentoPDF is an open-source PDF toolkit that you can either use through its hosted web version or self-host on your own server using Docker. Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick. All processing happens client-side in your browser, so even when you're running it on a server, the files never leave your machine. The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for. You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering. There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription. For someone deciding whether BentoPDF is worth their time, the short answer is yes, if your workflow revolves around form filling, annotations, and document management rather than direct text editing. More on that limitation later. BentoPDF offers a few installation options, including a bare-metal install, but the recommended and fastest route is Docker Compose. To set up BentoPDF, you need Docker installed before anything else. If you don't have it, download Docker Desktop , run the installer, and wait until the system tray icon shows Docker Desktop is running . On Windows, Docker will ask you to enable WSL 2 during setup. Accept that, restart if prompted, and you're good. Once Docker is ready, open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell. On macOS or Linux, the default terminal works. BentoPDF ships in two image variants: the standard version includes BentoPDF's marketing pages alongside the tools, while the "Simple Mode" image strips those out and shows only the tools. For internal or company use, Simple Mode is the cleaner option. The install steps are the same for both; you just use a different image tag. The fastest way to get BentoPDF running is a single command: For a more reliable setup that restarts automatically if your machine reboots, use Docker Compose instead. Create a new folder anywhere on your drive, open it in your terminal, and create a file called docker-compose.yml with the following content: Then run Docker compose up -d in the same folder. The -d flag runs it in the background so you can close the terminal without stopping BentoPDF. It will now survive reboots and start itself back up whenever Docker launches. If you eventually want BentoPDF accessible over the internet with a custom domain like pdf.yourdomain.com, you would pair it with a reverse proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager or Caddy, point a DNS record at your server's public IP, and request an SSL certificate so the connection is encrypted. That's a separate project and not strictly necessary for local or LAN use, but worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics. Docker Desktop is a one-click application for Windows, macOS, and Linux for easily building, running, and managing containerized applications. The biggest limitation is direct text editing. Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor. BentoPDF can't do that. Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document. If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor. There's also no native desktop or mobile app. BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it. That's part of its privacy appeal, but it means no offline experience and no app store install. And unlike Acrobat or PDFGear, there's no AI-powered summarization, which is consistent with its privacy-first stance, but worth noting if that's something you rely on. For my use case, though, none of these were deal-breakers. I didn't need a full-fledged editor. I needed a way to fill forms, annotate documents, and make all of that accessible to a team without uploading anything to a third-party service. And BentoPDF does exactly that. BentoPDF is a free, open-source, privacy-first PDF toolkit that runs entirely in your browser (or self-hosted), merging, splitting, compressing, converting, and editing PDFs with zero uploads or tracking. BentoPDF is a strong choice if you care more about privacy and control over where your PDFs are processed than having every feature under one roof. Yes, it doesn't have direct text editing, and a few other things like native apps, AI features, and enterprise-grade signing workflows might still be part of the roadmap and could take a while to land. But for form filling, annotations, compression, and format conversion on a server you own, it already does enough to replace a paid subscription. If anything, the fact that all processing stays client-side, even on a self-hosted instance, makes it one of the more privacy-respecting PDF tools I've tested. We want to hear from you. extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. sources.title: Crews forced to cut through security doors to battle West Side convenience store fire
passages: SAN ANTONIO - Firefighters had a tougher time getting into a West Side convenience store than putting out the fire itself early Saturday morning.
Crews had to cut through the doors before they could get to the flames.
When firefighters arrived, they found the store's metal security doors blocking their way inside.
The building's cinderblock walls helped keep the fire contained inside the store, but the damage was already done.

Crews had to cut through the doors before they could get to the flames. Once inside, firefighters quickly put out the fire. The building's cinderblock walls helped keep the fire contained inside the store, but the damage was already done. Investigators said an electrical issue sparked the fire. The shooting happened around 2 a.m. on March 15 at 1900 East Long Ave.According to the affidavit filed by Fort Worth police, Parish was a passenger in a black 2004 Ford Expedition and had been firing a tan handgun into the ground several times before the encounter. Investigators say Avila, who reportedly appeared intoxicated and possibly having a schizophrenic episode, approached the SUV at the intersection of East Long and Schwartz avenues because he was upset that Parish had been firing a weapon in the neighborhood.Witnesses and occupants of the vehicle told police that Avila was unarmed and stood on the left side of the SUV, yelling at Parish through the passenger window. When the driver reversed and tried to drive around Avila, he moved into the vehicle's path, forcing it to stop again.As Avila walked toward the front of the vehicle, the affidavit alleges that Parish stuck the tan pistol out of the window and fired one shot. Avila collapsed in a grassy median and died at the scene.The occupants of the vehicle initially left the scene but then made a U-turn to return and check if the man had been shot. Officers, alerted by the Real Time Crime Center, conducted an investigatory stop in the 2900 block of North Nichols and detained all five people inside the vehicle. Police found a black pistol and a tan pistol in plain view inside the vehicle.The investigating detective noted that no witnesses believed Avila was armed or attempting to assault anyone, saying Parish used deadly force despite not being threatened with imminent harm.Parish remains in custody on a murder charge.

Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO:ETH) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027. Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves. For many organizations, partnering with a regulated bank is the only option that meets their compliance requirements. Bitcoin and Ether prices barely moved after the news. Bitcoin is trading at approximately $81,497 as of October 17, down 0.7% in the past day, while Ether has dropped 0.8% to around $2,428. So, will Deutsche Bank's move encourage other big banks to follow suit, and could that influx of interest boost these cryptocurrencies' prices? Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro. In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set. This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions. However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets. BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York's financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies. U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services. State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date. While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage. Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products, yet prices have struggled. For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%. According to State Street's March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market. Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks' adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms. More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched. For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence. If Deutsche Bank's German launch arrives without a named client or disclosed assets in custody, it could be plumbing for demand that hasn't shown up yet. Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO:ETH) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027. Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. So, will Deutsche Bank's move encourage other big banks to follow suit, and could that influx of interest boost these cryptocurrencies' prices? Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro. In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set. This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions. However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets. BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York's financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies. U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services. State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date. While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage. Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products, yet prices have struggled. For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%. According to State Street's March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market. Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks' adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms. More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched. For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence. If Deutsche Bank's German launch arrives without a named client or disclosed assets in custody, it could be plumbing for demand that hasn't shown up yet. Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO:ETH) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.

Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves.
