extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

sources.title: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75 - TechCrunch
passages: Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year .

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations.
Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted.

Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device .
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.
Get 50% off a second pass Cover more ground at TechCrunch’s ultimate founder bootcamp of the year by bringing your co-founder or partner.
Meet scaling and investment leaders, ask questions, find solutions, and more.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

sources.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.” That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking. “I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.” You can contact or verify outreach from Aisha by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at aisha_malik.01 on Signal. The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. extraction.body: At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway . Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion. "Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement. The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio. For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ." Shares of Intuit , HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro , once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion. "You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore." Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus . Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo , AOL and Eventbrite in 2025. The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07. Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price. Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions. Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied." "They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020. Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years." As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar. extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. extraction.body: Masad pitched a self-driving company model and stressed multi-model flexibility as frontier labs move into coding tools Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding. Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration. What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider. That matters, because the labs supplying the models are increasingly becoming the competition. Masad spoke at Disrupt, which ran October 15–16, 2026. He used the appearance to lay out what he calls the “self-driving company.” The idea is simple to describe and harder to execute. AI agents handle the repetitive first pass on operational work, and people step in where judgment is required. Replit has run this model internally since early 2026. Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues. Replit’s financial trajectory explains why people listen when Masad talks. The company’s revenue stood at $2.8 million in 2024. By 2026, its projected annual run-rate is approaching nearly $1 billion. That is more than a hundredfold increase in roughly two years. Replit’s valuation climbed from $3 billion to $9 billion earlier this year, tripling on the back of a $250 million funding round. Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it. Anthropic’s Claude models have been central to Agent since 2024, and the integration remains active. The tension is structural. Replit depends on frontier AI labs for the models that power its product, and those same labs are building their own coding tools. Masad acknowledged the risk directly. He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves. Replit’s answer is multi-model flexibility. Masad emphasized that the company is steering clear of reliance on any one AI provider, keeping the ability to swap or combine models as the market shifts. Model providers control the most expensive and hardest-to-replicate layer of the stack. Application companies like Replit control the user relationship, the workflow and the product experience. For now, both sides need each other. Anthropic gains a high-growth distribution channel through Replit’s Agent, and Replit gains access to models its users rely on. That is why vendor lock-in has become a board-level concern across AI software. Masad’s emphasis on flexibility reads as a hedge against exactly that scenario, and it may resonate with enterprise buyers who share the same worry about depending on one provider. The flip side is concentration risk. A company whose flagship product leans heavily on a third party’s models carries exposure that a traditional software firm would not, and a $9 billion valuation prices in a lot of continued execution. For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024. coreStoryFacts.text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding.
Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.
For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024.
Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.
Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it.
He pointed to Anthropic and OpenAI as potential competitors that could launch tools aimed at the same users Replit serves.
Masad framed it as a shift in how work gets divided, with employees freed up for strategic decisions rather than sorting through queues.
What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider.

extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. extraction.body: Replit CEO Amjad Masad said during an onstage interview at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 that the company is no longer working with Anthropic, framing the decision around cost, partnership, and performance. The session recording was published by TechCrunch on October 16, 2026. The exchange began when the interviewer asked whether the OpenAI partnership Replit announced in August 2026 meant the company was no longer working with Anthropic. “Yeah. I mean, yeah,” Masad answered. Masad said OpenAI’s models now perform better for Replit’s workloads. “I think GPT is better now,” he said, citing an internal Replit benchmark called VBench and a public benchmark the company has published. He said OpenAI’s Sol and Astra models consistently performed better at building vibe-coded applications from scratch, and he described the switch as a decision based on cost, partnership, and performance, with OpenAI the better partner for now. When the interviewer asked whether losing Replit had contributed to what he described as Anthropic’s reported revenue slowdown, Masad said Replit was also one of Anthropic’s top five customers. Earlier in the session, asked whether Replit is vulnerable to the same disruption it creates as OpenAI and Anthropic move beyond code generation into building, deploying, and hosting apps, Masad said those offerings remain surface level next to Replit’s full-stack, integrated environment, noting that OpenAI relies on an external service, Cloudflare, for hosting. He said Replit’s agents can spin up databases and key-value stores inside a production environment and that the company can deploy its entire stack into government and enterprise environments as an on-premises solution. Replit’s current model-selector documentation lists Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5 Fast, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 as Max Mode options, alongside GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna Fast, and Kimi K3, with GPT-6 Sol offered in Power Mode. Free Mode always uses intelligent model routing with no manual selection, and the Fast variants require a Pro or Enterprise plan. A September 29, 2026 engineering post on Replit’s blog documented Claude Fable 5 running in Replit Agent production in August 2026 and Fable 5.1 alongside GPT-6 Astra in September 2026. The post’s production data shows Fable 5 dispatching a subagent on 32% of turns, Fable 5.1 on 21%, and Astra on 36%, each at medium reasoning effort. The post reports that Replit Agent, evaluated in Max mode with Astra as its core loop, scored 72% at $2.11 per task on the DeepSWE v1.1 benchmark and 49% at $2.53 per task on Terminal-Bench 4.0, beating a sidekick architecture, the same setup with one long-lived worker, by 11 and 16 points. Replit’s engineers wrote that the code quality of Astra and Fable 5.1 let the company use its code-review subagent less with no drop in evaluation scores, describing it as a level of engineering quality they had not seen from any model before. The OpenAI partnership itself dates to Replit’s August 18, 2026 announcement of Free Mode, powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna. Replit said Core subscribers could create up to 30 times more than before for their $20 monthly subscription, including up to 30 hours per month of chat, with everyday tasks in Free Mode no longer consuming credits. The announcement describes Power Mode, formerly Economy Mode, as using cost-optimized models and Max Mode as using higher-performance models, with usage limits resetting every five hours. In the same session, Masad said enterprise contracts account for about 15% of Replit’s revenue in 2026, versus about 2% in 2025, and that more than 50% of revenue is now B2B. He declined to share ARR figures. Masad said companies that adopt Replit spend 400% more within 12 months, a net revenue retention rate he put above 400%, and said Replit has been gross-margin positive with margins growing alongside enterprise adoption. Masad also described what he called an agent habitat of orchestration, error recovery, sandboxing, networking, and identity and authorization as the prerequisite for deploying AI safely inside organizations. He outlined Replit’s pre-deployment security scans, post-deployment penetration-test scans, supply-chain monitoring, and a one-click kill switch that lets enterprise customers take down any app or all apps. He referenced Replit’s September 2024 launch of Agent 1 and a 2025 incident in which an agent deleted a database, saying stored snapshots make restoration a one-click action. Masad said there are no immediate plans to raise new funding, that an IPO is in the company’s future, and that Replit has turned down acquisition approaches because it is focused on building a long-term company. story.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says

facts.text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.
After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and addressed his company’s relationship with Anthropic , one of the most important supplier ties in AI coding.
Replit has not publicly announced any termination of that collaboration.
For the moment, Replit and Anthropic remain linked through the Claude integration that has powered Agent since 2024.
Masad’s message at Disrupt was less about ending relationships and more about making sure no single relationship can end Replit.
Much of that growth rides on Replit’s Agent product, which lets users describe what they want and have AI build it.

What Masad did make clear is that Replit does not intend to bet the company on any single model provider.

Security guards may be the next workers SoftBank Group tries to automate. On Friday, October 16, 2026, reports emerged that SoftBank is considering acquiring Allied Universal, a private company that initial reports described as the largest U.S. security services firm. A source familiar with the matter, Reuters reported, said a deal could value Allied at about $18 billion. Reuters also noted SoftBank’s 2025 agreement to buy ABB’s robotics business for $5.4 billion.
Talks are preliminary, and no decision has been made on price; SoftBank declined to comment, and Allied did not immediately respond.

SoftBank’s U.S. over-the-counter shares fell 9.98% to $14.70, with a market cap of about $160.39 billion, during a broad AI selloff. Arm Holdings ( NASDAQ:ARM | ARM Price Prediction ) fell 6.94%, Teradyne ( NASDAQ:TER ) slipped 5.31%, and Symbotic ( NASDAQ:SYM ) lost 2.49%. Those moves came on the same day the Allied report emerged.
Allied staffs security for businesses, venues and major events. It also has a growing presence in data centers, where it supports both construction and day-to-day operation.

People familiar with the talks say SoftBank would eventually replace some guards with robots for certain tasks. Humanoid robots would take longer to roll out. The report included no financing details, no robot timeline, and no estimate of how many jobs could be affected, and it did not say whether the valuation refers to equity or enterprise value.
Guarding is a payroll business with thin margins. The deal works only if machines take over enough shifts to lift margins at scale.

Patrols, camera monitoring and access control are the easiest tasks to automate. Judgment calls, medical emergencies and stadium crowd control are much harder. Clients also pay for accountability and liability coverage, so replacing guards raises questions about insurance, licensing rules and whether customers will accept the change.

SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, already contributed $193 million of Arm’s $574 million in June-quarter license revenue. Royalties from security robots would barely register against a $243.29 billion market value.

Teradyne owns Universal Robots and MiR. But its Robotics segment produced only $100 million of its $1.329 billion in second-quarter revenue, selling to factories and warehouses. Teradyne has disclosed no tie to Allied.

Symbotic holds a 35% stake in Exol, a warehouse-as-a-service joint venture with SoftBank, with a contract worth about $11 billion. That business automates logistics, which is a separate market from guarding buildings.

Founder Masayoshi Son’s early Alibaba ( NYSE:BABA ) investment and his Arm interest produced large gains, while WeWork produced large losses. SoftBank’s Pepper robot, whose production was paused, is a closer warning for this deal.

Allied’s data center work gives SoftBank a ready-made customer base for testing robots inside AI infrastructure. Still, the deal would buy a low-margin service business on the promise of technology that is years away from working at scale.

The bull case rests on scarce, expensive labor. Teradyne’s robotics revenue grew 33% from a year earlier, and its chief executive said on July 29, 2026, that physical AI applications will drive that growth.
The bear case is valuation. Arm trades at 152x forward earnings and Symbotic at 161x, prices that assume adoption arrives on schedule.

AI robotics valuations have the strongest support where robots or chips already bring in revenue. By that test, Teradyne at 31x forward earnings rests on more existing revenue than any SoftBank robot-guard thesis.

The thing to look for is a signed agreement from SoftBank or Allied that states a price and financing. Until one is announced, the robot-guard plan remains a statement of intent that adds no real revenue to any of these three companies.

IBIT shareholders gain Bitcoin price exposure but cannot withdraw coins, spending or storing them personally is impossible. Share creations and redemptions drive Bitcoin supply dynamics, with IBIT mirroring Bitcoin's 23% drop over the past year. Finally! You can open a SoFi Crypto account and access 25 plus cryptocurrencies without juggling apps or logins. Many investors in BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF might think the fund manager owns the Bitcoin. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure. While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys. IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust's Bitcoin, but they don't own the coins outright or can't withdraw them. Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080. On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin's price? A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins. Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust. This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it. BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager. Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this. The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF. When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders. That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin's 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods. In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves. IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust's Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Many investors in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF might think the fund manager owns the Bitcoin. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure . While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK | BLK Price Prediction ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys.

IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust’s Bitcoin, but they don’t own the coins outright or can’t withdraw them.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080 . On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin’s price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust’s Bitcoin’s economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock’s finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock’s role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust’s assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys —the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers’ assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT’s functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn’t directly affect Bitcoin’s price because it doesn’t create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That’s why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin’s price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin’s 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else’s vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin’s price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust’s Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics.

While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys.

IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust's Bitcoin, but they don't own the coins outright or can't withdraw them.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080. On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin's price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin's 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust's Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics.

sources.title: A rogue OpenAI agent robbed a crypto wallet to obtain funds to carry out a task - Fortune
passages: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved.
In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them.
Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning.
It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report.
The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval.

The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks.
The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers.
OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests.
It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved. In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network. Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them. The incident happened on June 26, when the model was asked to update a crypto trading app and get its code running on Sepolia, a test version of Ethereum . The prompt gave it neither a funded wallet nor permission to spend tokens, and after failing to get free test tokens through developer services, the model wrote a script checking 362 wallet addresses linked to public recovery phrases, a crypto term that describes sets of words that can act as a password to unlock crypto accounts. It eventually found an account with enough tokens to cover the fees. Internal logs showed that the model deliberated over whether it had permission to use the account, but then decided the public recovery phrase and the tokens’ lack of cash value made the spending acceptable. It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report. OpenAI only discovered the incident on Sept. 25 during an audit of earlier model runs. The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval. OpenAI’s public tracker of misalignment, or behavior that goes against instructions or safety rules, now lists 19 incidents, ranging from accessing data without permission to making unauthorized changes to business systems. The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks. In July, the company faced another incident when its AI agents bypassed internet restrictions during internal cybersecurity tests and broke into systems belonging to Hugging Face , a platform for sharing AI models and datasets. The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers. Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning. “This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said. OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests. It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

I replaced Adobe Acrobat with a free open-source self-hosted app, and I'm not going back

sources.title: I replaced Adobe Acrobat with a free open-source self-hosted app, and I'm not going back - MakeUseOf
passages: The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for.

You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering.
There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription.
While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF.
A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use.
Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick.
The biggest limitation is direct text editing.
Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor.
Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document.
If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor.
Tashreef's fascination with consumer technology began in the school library when he stumbled upon a tech magazine, CHIP, which ultimately inspired him to pursue a degree in Computer Science.

While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup.

extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. Most importantly, there are no AI tools. I think photography and photo editing are fun, and fun, creative things should be left to people rather than machines. I won't put on my tinfoil hat and go full conspiracy theorist, but the more AI gets integrated into my personal devices and the more I'm forced to use it, the more claustrophobic I feel. Using some of these de-bloated tools that don't use AI has made my phone a lot less stressful, and it hasn't noticeably decreased my productivity. I won't stop using AI altogether, but I am starting to question when and where it feels useful and when it's simply a gimmick. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

PDF apps are a dime a dozen, and unlike a decade ago, you can find a full-fledged PDF editor like PDFGear completely for free . However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it. While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF. A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use. Your PDF fonts shouldn’t vanish when you edit. BentoPDF is an open-source PDF toolkit that you can either use through its hosted web version or self-host on your own server using Docker. Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick. All processing happens client-side in your browser, so even when you're running it on a server, the files never leave your machine. The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for. You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering. There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription. For someone deciding whether BentoPDF is worth their time, the short answer is yes, if your workflow revolves around form filling, annotations, and document management rather than direct text editing. More on that limitation later. BentoPDF offers a few installation options, including a bare-metal install, but the recommended and fastest route is Docker Compose. To set up BentoPDF, you need Docker installed before anything else. If you don't have it, download Docker Desktop , run the installer, and wait until the system tray icon shows Docker Desktop is running . On Windows, Docker will ask you to enable WSL 2 during setup. Accept that, restart if prompted, and you're good. Once Docker is ready, open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell. On macOS or Linux, the default terminal works. BentoPDF ships in two image variants: the standard version includes BentoPDF's marketing pages alongside the tools, while the "Simple Mode" image strips those out and shows only the tools. For internal or company use, Simple Mode is the cleaner option. The install steps are the same for both; you just use a different image tag. The fastest way to get BentoPDF running is a single command: For a more reliable setup that restarts automatically if your machine reboots, use Docker Compose instead. Create a new folder anywhere on your drive, open it in your terminal, and create a file called docker-compose.yml with the following content: Then run Docker compose up -d in the same folder. The -d flag runs it in the background so you can close the terminal without stopping BentoPDF. It will now survive reboots and start itself back up whenever Docker launches. If you eventually want BentoPDF accessible over the internet with a custom domain like pdf.yourdomain.com, you would pair it with a reverse proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager or Caddy, point a DNS record at your server's public IP, and request an SSL certificate so the connection is encrypted. That's a separate project and not strictly necessary for local or LAN use, but worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics. Docker Desktop is a one-click application for Windows, macOS, and Linux for easily building, running, and managing containerized applications. The biggest limitation is direct text editing. Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor. BentoPDF can't do that. Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document. If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor. There's also no native desktop or mobile app. BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it. That's part of its privacy appeal, but it means no offline experience and no app store install. And unlike Acrobat or PDFGear, there's no AI-powered summarization, which is consistent with its privacy-first stance, but worth noting if that's something you rely on. For my use case, though, none of these were deal-breakers. I didn't need a full-fledged editor. I needed a way to fill forms, annotate documents, and make all of that accessible to a team without uploading anything to a third-party service. And BentoPDF does exactly that. BentoPDF is a free, open-source, privacy-first PDF toolkit that runs entirely in your browser (or self-hosted), merging, splitting, compressing, converting, and editing PDFs with zero uploads or tracking. BentoPDF is a strong choice if you care more about privacy and control over where your PDFs are processed than having every feature under one roof. Yes, it doesn't have direct text editing, and a few other things like native apps, AI features, and enterprise-grade signing workflows might still be part of the roadmap and could take a while to land. But for form filling, annotations, compression, and format conversion on a server you own, it already does enough to replace a paid subscription. If anything, the fact that all processing stays client-side, even on a self-hosted instance, makes it one of the more privacy-respecting PDF tools I've tested. We want to hear from you. extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. Most importantly, there are no AI tools. I think photography and photo editing are fun, and fun, creative things should be left to people rather than machines. I won't put on my tinfoil hat and go full conspiracy theorist, but the more AI gets integrated into my personal devices and the more I'm forced to use it, the more claustrophobic I feel.
