passages: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools.

Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder.

I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead.

This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking.

I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security.

I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me.

Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you.

The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service.

Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it.

Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull.

Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. I won't stop using AI altogether, but I am starting to question when and where it feels useful and when it's simply a gimmick.

facts.text: The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for.

You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering.
There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription.
While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF.
A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use.
Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick.
The biggest limitation is direct text editing.
Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor.
Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document.
If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor.

Since 2012, Tashreef has professionally authored over a thousand how-to articles, contributing to Windows Report and How-To Geek.
He currently focuses on Microsoft Windows content at MakeUseOf, which he has been using since 2007.
BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it.

However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it.

passages: SAN ANTONIO - Firefighters had a tougher time getting into a West Side convenience store than putting out the fire itself early Saturday morning.

The building's cinderblock walls helped keep the fire contained inside the store, but the damage was already done.

extraction.body: SAN ANTONIO - Firefighters had a tougher time getting into a West Side convenience store than putting out the fire itself early Saturday morning. The fire broke out around 12:30 a.m. at the Z21 Food Mart near Ruiz and North Sabinas streets. When firefighters arrived, they found the store's metal security doors blocking their way inside. Crews had to cut through the doors before they could get to the flames. Once inside, firefighters quickly put out the fire. The building's cinderblock walls helped keep the fire contained inside the store, but the damage was already done. Investigators said an electrical issue sparked the fire. The store was closed at the time, and no one was injured.

When the driver reversed and tried to drive around Avila, he moved into the vehicle's path, forcing it to stop again.As Avila walked toward the front of the vehicle, the affidavit alleges that Parish stuck the tan pistol out of the window and fired one shot. Avila collapsed in a grassy median and died at the scene.The occupants of the vehicle initially left the scene but then made a U-turn to return and check if the man had been shot. Officers, alerted by the Real Time Crime Center, conducted an investigatory stop in the 2900 block of North Nichols and detained all five people inside the vehicle. Police found a black pistol and a tan pistol in plain view inside the vehicle.The investigating detective noted that no witnesses believed Avila was armed or attempting to assault anyone, saying Parish used deadly force despite not being threatened with imminent harm.Parish remains in custody on a murder charge.

When the driver reversed and tried to drive around Avila, he moved into the vehicle's path, forcing it to stop again.As Avila walked toward the front of the vehicle, the affidavit alleges that Parish stuck the tan pistol out of the window and fired one shot.
Avila collapsed in a grassy median and died at the scene.The occupants of the vehicle initially left the scene but then made a U-turn to return and check if the man had been shot.
Officers, alerted by the Real Time Crime Center, conducted an investigatory stop in the 2900 block of North Nichols and detained all five people inside the vehicle.

Police found a black pistol and a tan pistol in plain view inside the vehicle.The investigating detective noted that no witnesses believed Avila was armed or attempting to assault anyone, saying Parish used deadly force despite not being threatened with imminent harm.Parish remains in custody on a murder charge.

extraction.body: The above button links to Coinbase. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Deutsche Bank will hold Bitcoin and Ether for institutional clients in Germany within weeks, with Asian expansion set for 2027. Bank custody adds access but not buyers. Bitcoin fell 23% and Ether 37% despite a year of major institutions launching new crypto products. Easing Basel Committee capital rules and client demand for consolidated holdings are pushing more major banks toward crypto custody services. Finally! You can open a SoFi Crypto account and access 25 plus cryptocurrencies without juggling apps or logins. Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO:ETH) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027. Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves. For many organizations, partnering with a regulated bank is the only option that meets their compliance requirements. Bitcoin and Ether prices barely moved after the news. Bitcoin is trading at approximately $81,497 as of October 17, down 0.7% in the past day, while Ether has dropped 0.8% to around $2,428. So, will Deutsche Bank's move encourage other big banks to follow suit, and could that influx of interest boost these cryptocurrencies' prices? Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro. In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set. This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions. However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets. BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York's financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies. U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services. State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date. While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage. Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products, yet prices have struggled. For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%. According to State Street's March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market. Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks' adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms. More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched. For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO:ETH) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank's corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.

Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves. For many organizations, partnering with a regulated bank is the only option that meets their compliance requirements.

Bitcoin and Ether prices barely moved after the news. Bitcoin is trading at approximately $81,497 as of October 17, down 0.7% in the past day, while Ether has dropped 0.8% to around $2,428. So, will Deutsche Bank's move encourage other big banks to follow suit, and could that influx of interest boost these cryptocurrencies' prices?

Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro.

In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set.

This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions.

However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets.

BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York's financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies.

U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services.

State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date.

While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage.

Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products, yet prices have struggled. For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%.

According to State Street's March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks' adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms.

More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched.

In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins. Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it. BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager. Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this. The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF. When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders. That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves. IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust's Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics. Many investors in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF might think the fund manager owns the Bitcoin. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure . While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK | BLK Price Prediction ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys.

IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust’s Bitcoin, but they don’t own the coins outright or can’t withdraw them.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080 . On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin’s price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust’s Bitcoin’s economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock’s finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock’s role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust’s assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys —the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers’ assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT’s functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn’t directly affect Bitcoin’s price because it doesn’t create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That’s why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin’s price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin’s 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else’s vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin’s price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust’s Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080. On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin's price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. AI models mostly run on matrix multiplication (“matmul”): multiplying enormous grids of numbers over and over. A GPU does that math by pushing electrons through billions of transistors, which burns power and throws off heat. A photonic chip encodes numbers in beams of light and lets them interact as they pass through optical components, so the answer comes out as the light crosses the chip. That gives you the speed and energy appeal.

Shkreli’s cautions carry real weight. Neural networks also need nonlinear steps between multiplications (functions that decide which signals pass forward), and light handles those poorly. Models also need memory to hold their weights and data, and that storage remains electronic. Any photonic core still needs conventional silicon wrapped around it.

For TRX, the key indicator will be the stablecoin supply, since a pattern of weekly declines could dampen its core demand. By comparison, Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) fell 9.3% over the same stretch, hitting a low of $2,313 on October 15, down from a peak of $2,807 on September 21.

Since then, TRON has remained stable. As of October 17, TRX trades at $0.34, up 1.3% over the past week. Meanwhile, Ethereum is priced at $2,428, down 2.6%. This raises the question: Is TRX’s steadier price a better investment, or does Ethereum’s deeper discount make it more attractive?

Among the major cryptocurrencies we track, only four posted gains over the past two weeks. Besides TRON, NEAR ( CRYPTO:NEAR ) rose 8.6%, Polkadot ( CRYPTO:DOT ) rose 3.4%, and Monero ( CRYPTO:XMR ), known for its privacy features, gained 3.2%.

Although TRON’s gain was the smallest, its stability stands out more than its growth. Through October 16, TRX rose 1% over seven days and fell 0.03% over the past month, meaning it has seen very little fluctuation.
In stark contrast, Ethereum has faced more volatility. While ETH was up 26.3% over the past 60 days through October 16, it has dropped 18.4% year-to-date and 36.9% from one year ago.

The two cryptocurrencies also differ significantly in size. Ethereum ranks second by market capitalization at $296.61 billion, nearly nine times TRON’s $31.83 billion, which ranks eighth. In trading volume, Ethereum saw $11.59 billion in 24-hour trading, about 36 times TRON’s $318 million.

Stablecoins are cryptocurrency tokens pegged to the U.S. dollar and are widely used for quick transfers between wallets and exchanges. Both TRON and Ethereum host a significant amount of stablecoins compared to other blockchains. According to DeFiLlama’s October 2026 rankings, Ethereum leads in stablecoin supply, with TRON second and well ahead of every other network.

However, TRON’s stablecoin base relies heavily on Tether’s dollar token, which traders and businesses in emerging markets use for low-cost transfers. In contrast, Ethereum has a larger and more diverse stablecoin base with several dollar-pegged tokens.

This payment role supports the TRX price: every transaction on TRON consumes network resources, which users access by either staking TRX (locking up coins to help maintain the network) or paying transaction fees in TRX. Steady payment activity creates consistent demand for the coin, regardless of broader market movements. Recently, DeFiLlama has reported a slight increase in TRON’s stablecoin supply over the past week, while Ethereum’s supply has dipped.

TRX is currently trading 22.3% below its all-time high of $0.43, reached on December 3, 2024, meaning holders have retained most of their investment value since that peak. However, this smaller discount leaves limited potential for a quick rebound, as TRX would need to rise nearly 29% to set a new record.

In contrast, Ethereum trades 50.9% below its August 2025 peak of $4,946. This deeper discount reflects a year of consistent selling . Still, ETH benefits from a larger stablecoin supply, the second-highest market cap in cryptocurrency, and much higher trading volume, allowing larger investors to buy and sell without greatly affecting the price.
In summary, TRX provides stability tied to one primary function—dollar payments—while ETH offers a broader network with greater volatility at about half its peak value.

At these price levels, Ethereum appears to offer more upside potential, while TRON provides greater stability. Over the past two weeks, TRX has held steady during market downturns. However, ETH’s 50.9% gap from its all-time high grants it more room for recovery. Of course, this upside comes with increased volatility, as ETH dropped 17.6% from its September high to its October low.

For ETH to recover, it needs to stay above its October 15 low of $2,313 and reclaim the $2,807 peak from September 21. If it falls below $2,313 , the argument for TRON’s stability may tip. For TRX, the key indicator will be the stablecoin supply, since a pattern of weekly declines could dampen its core demand. Conversely, if TRX surpasses $0.43, it may signal a surge in payment demand and attract new buyers.

passages: Ethereum dropped 10% in October to $2,428, yet 59% of social media posts remain bullish, reflecting more optimism than Bitcoin's sentiment despite ETH underperforming BTC.
According to Santiment, a prominent crypto analytics firm that monitors social media discussions and blockchain activities, 59.1% of posts about ETH over the latest 24 hours are positive.
It appears that the crowd might indeed be too early.
Optimistic voices in the community contrast sharply with the outflow of funds, and historical trends suggest financial actions usually carry more weight than social sentiment.
Santiment's framework also suggests current Ethereum sentiment could be a warning sign; those buying solely on this mood may be entering ahead of further selling pressure.
In contrast to bullish sentiment on social media, fund investors appear to be withdrawing.
The U.S. spot Ether ETFs, which trade on U.S. stock exchanges and hold ETH directly, experienced net outflows on five out of six trading days from October 8 to 15, as reported by SoSoValue.
The most significant outflow occurred on October 14, with $130 million exiting the funds, followed by another $60 million on October 15.
For the crowd's optimism to prove correct, ETF flows would need to turn positive for several sessions, nudging cumulative net inflow back above $13.3 billion.

Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) has dropped 10.2% since October 1, 2026, but social media sentiment remains optimistic. According to Santiment, a prominent crypto analytics firm that monitors social media discussions and blockchain activities, 59.1% of posts about ETH over the latest 24 hours are positive.

Ethereum started October at $2,705 and is now trading around $2,428 as of October 17, down 0.8% in the last 24 hours. The cryptocurrency peaked at $2,777 on October 2 before plummeting to a low of $2,313 on October 15, a day when ETH led the market in liquidations , the forced closures of leveraged trades that ran out of collateral.
While sentiment appears hopeful, the persistent decline raises one question. Is the crowd too early on Ethereum?

Santiment’s analysis shows that 59.1% of ETH posts are bullish, compared with 57.9% for Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ). Furthermore, Santiment’s intensity metric—which measures how strongly posts express sentiment—ranks ETH at 54.1%, while Bitcoin scores 52.2%. This indicates that, despite ETH’s weaker price, its community remains more optimistic than Bitcoin’s.
In the past month, ETH has lost 1.1%, while Bitcoin has gained 6.8%. Additionally, for 2026, ETH is down 18.4% compared to Bitcoin’s 6.8% decline.
Sentiment readings reflect what people say, not necessarily what they do with their assets. A participant can express bullish sentiment one day and sell their ETH the next.

Santiment has consistently viewed crowd optimism during a downturn as a potential warning, whereas fear can indicate more favorable entry points. When most holders remain hopeful for a rebound, it often suggests that those likely to panic and sell have not yet exited their positions, potentially leading to further declines.

Much of the current optimism may stem from Ethereum’s summer rally, as ETH is still up 26.7% over 60 days from $1,917 on August 18. This is likely fresh in many holders’ minds, overshadowing the current downturn.

In contrast to bullish sentiment on social media, fund investors appear to be withdrawing. The U.S. spot Ether ETFs, which trade on U.S. stock exchanges and hold ETH directly, experienced net outflows on five out of six trading days from October 8 to 15, as reported by SoSoValue. The most significant outflow occurred on October 14, with $130 million exiting the funds, followed by another $60 million on October 15.

A brief inflow on October 13 lasted only a day . The cumulative net inflow—the total amount invested in the funds since their launch minus withdrawals—dropped from $13.3 billion on October 8 to $13.0 billion on October 15, reflecting a decrease of approximately $306 million. Total ETF assets stood at $15.3 billion on October 15.

Interactive Brokers, one of the largest online brokers in the U.S., has enabled clients to stake Ethereum , which involves locking ETH to help secure the network in exchange for rewards. This new option might attract new buyers eventually, but the ETF flows have not yet shown any sign of recovery.

It appears that the crowd might indeed be too early. Optimistic voices in the community contrast sharply with the outflow of funds, and historical trends suggest financial actions usually carry more weight than social sentiment. Santiment’s framework also suggests current Ethereum sentiment could be a warning sign; those buying solely on this mood may be entering ahead of further selling pressure.

For the crowd’s optimism to prove correct, ETF flows would need to turn positive for several sessions, nudging cumulative net inflow back above $13.3 billion. ETH would also need to close above $2,705 to target the $2,777 high. If negative flows persist and ETH dips below its $2,313 low, sentiment may shift from hope to fear, which, according to Santiment, could offer a more advantageous entry point for buyers.

Fundstrat co-founder Tom Lee described the cryptocurrency market as “a coiled spring.” He believes that while prices have dipped, the reasons to invest in these assets remain strong. A coiled spring holds energy when compressed, and Lee sees the latest crypto pullback as a similar situation.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at about $81,497, down 3.6% over the past two weeks but up 7.8% over the last 30 days. Bitcoin hit the lower end of its trading range on October 14 after investors grew more cautious.
So, which major coins have pulled back the most, and which declines might be a temporary pause in an upward trend?

Lee compares cryptocurrencies to chip stocks and AI cloud companies, suggesting that all three are like a coiled spring if their underlying fundamentals remain sound. He notes that these assets have “pulled back to support levels.” A support level is a price point where previous buyers stepped in, often stalling price declines.

Lee emphasizes that when strong fundamentals persist and market sentiment turns sour, investors get a favorable risk-reward scenario. This means the potential upside outweighs the possible downsides. Market fear can quickly drive prices down, creating a buying opportunity for those with a more optimistic view.

Fundstrat strategist Mark Newton has taken this analysis a step further, suggesting the market could bottom out within a few days. While Lee did not specify a price target for any coin, he has suggested that Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) is nearing the end of its prolonged decline against Bitcoin .

Among the top coins, Hedera ( CRYPTO:HBAR ) has seen the largest decline, dropping 17.8% in the last two weeks. This pullback follows a substantial 27% jump after an IBM cloud announcement on September 28. The table below shows prices as of October 16, including Bitcoin and Ethereum for comparison.

All seven coins in this analysis lost value over the past 24 hours, with smaller coins typically showing steeper declines during a pullback. Bitcoin’s relatively mild 3.6% two-week drop stands out compared to the larger decreases observed in Uniswap ( CRYPTO:UNI ), Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ), Litecoin ( CRYPTO:LTC ), and Aave ( CRYPTO:AAVE ).
Despite these pullbacks, all seven coins posted positive returns over the past 30 days, as most losses followed a strong price surge from September into October.

Aave, a lending protocol that facilitates borrowing and lending of cryptocurrencies, displays a chart that most suggests a reset. The coin fell 13.5% over the past two weeks but remains up 32.5% over 30 days, indicating that this drop is likely profit-taking during an upward trend.
Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap show similar patterns; each has given back only part of its monthly gains, with Litecoin up 17.1%, Hedera 14.9%, and Uniswap 14.3%.
Conversely, Stellar appears to have a weaker outlook. XLM has dropped 15.3% over two weeks and has only gained 1.0% this month, trading 79.4% below its all-time high of $0.88 in January 2018.

Ethereum mirrors this trend, with little room left to run, posting a 1.3% monthly gain and trading 51.1% below its previous peak of $4,946 from August 2025. Bitcoin is also well below its high, down 35.4% from its October 2025 record of $126,080 .

In the current crypto pullback, Lee’s description seems to fit Aave, Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap more than Stellar or Ethereum. The first four have experienced pullbacks after strong monthly performance, suggesting their declines could be a temporary correction in a rising trend. In contrast, Stellar and Ethereum show diminishing momentum, indicating their drops might signal a weakening trend.

Ultimately, Bitcoin could steer the altcoins. Historically, altcoins tend to rally only after Bitcoin makes a move , and Bitcoin has recorded only two down months in October since 2013 . If Bitcoin can hold its October 16 low of $80,761 and Aave rises above $165, Lee’s theory may hold true. However, if Bitcoin falls below $80,761 and Stellar’s 30-day gain turns negative, the coiled spring may only apply to a select few coins.

Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro. In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. U.S. crude reached $102 a barrel on October 14, 2026—its highest price since mid-September—while Brent crude, the global oil standard, climbed above $106.

Bitcoin trades at $81,497, down 1.5% over the previous week but still up 6.8% over the last month. Notably, Bitcoin also traded through a similar spike in crude oil in September, which could hint at similar movements in the current landscape.

Escalating tensions in the Middle East are driving the recent rise in oil prices. Specifically, Iran has increased its attacks near the Strait of Hormuz , a critical route for global oil transport. In addition, Ukraine has vowed to continue striking Russian refineries. The Strait of Hormuz, lying between Iran and Oman, is crucial since a significant portion of the world’s oil passes through it.

As these tensions persisted into mid-October, oil prices surged. For instance, on October 14, crude prices jumped significantly following attacks in Saudi Arabia and new strategies launched by Iran against tankers. By October 16, Brent oil continued to climb as regional pressure mounted.

Within a week, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil posted a nearly $7 increase, marking a 7.3% rise. According to federal data, WTI peaked at $107 on September 15, its highest level since at least July, but then fell roughly 20% to $85 by September 25 before starting to climb again.

Interestingly, Bitcoin reacted to rising oil prices in September. It closed at $81,264 on September 3, when WTI was around $93 per barrel, but then fell 7% to $75,584 on September 15, coinciding with oil’s peak. During that particular trading session, Bitcoin dipped to as low as $74,888.

On September 17, when WTI oil was priced at $103, Bitcoin closed higher at $76,349. As oil prices retreated the next day, Bitcoin bounced back to close at $80,875 on September 18, as WTI eased to about $101. By September 21, when WTI fell to $97, Bitcoin hit an intraday high of $87,397, marking its best performance of that month.

Despite a minor cooling off afterward, Bitcoin held most of its gains, closing at $84,849 on October 1, while WTI hovered just below $100 . However, once oil climbed back over $100, Bitcoin fell to $81,566 on October 14, the same day WTI reached about $102. If history is any guide, Bitcoin’s next upward movement may hinge on when oil prices begin to decline again.

High oil prices often feed into inflation. When crude becomes expensive, it raises costs for gasoline, shipping, and nearly everything that requires transportation, thereby exerting inflationary pressure . This elevated inflation typically keeps borrowing costs higher, which can make speculative assets like Bitcoin less appealing to many investors.

Additionally, when geopolitical tensions drive oil prices up, risk appetite tends to decline. Investors often shy away from volatile assets, and during these times, Bitcoin frequently trades in tandem with tech stocks. For example, on October 16, tech stocks sold off sharply as oil prices surged.

Nevertheless, the relationship between oil and Bitcoin can also diverge. Some investors turn to Bitcoin as a n inflation hedge because of its fixed supply. A prolonged spike in oil prices that amplifies costs could eventually attract new buyers to Bitcoin. However, in September, Bitcoin behaved more like a speculative asset, declining as oil prices surged and recovering as they receded.

The previous trend suggests yes, but the downturn lasted only as long as the oil-price spike. Bitcoin dropped to $75,584 on the day WTI peaked, then rebounded about 16% to $87,397 by September 21, when crude fell below $100. Bitcoin is currently trading at $81,497, while WTI is around $102 and Brent is above $106. Although Bitcoin has gained 26.1% over the past 60 days, it remains down 6.8% for 2026.

News from the Strait of Hormuz could influence Bitcoin as much as any crypto-related headlines in the coming weeks. Investors should watch Bitcoin’s September 17 close of $76,349. If oil stays above $100 and Bitcoin closes below that threshold, Bitcoin might repeat its September decline and revisit the $74,888 low from that time.

sources.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
passages: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents.
In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity.
Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

sources.body: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. extraction.body: Samsung's Auto Blocker keeps threats at bay, but it can also get in your way. If you own a Samsung Galaxy phone running One UI 6.0 or later, you may have a built-in security feature called Auto Blocker working in the background without even realizing it. Enabled by default on devices that ship with One UI 6.1.1 or later, it filters out apps, USB commands and messages that could put your device at risk without you even having to lift a finger. For most people, that's a super useful layer of protection in a world where threats are extremely common and can come from apps, a public charging cable or images you get in a text. But Auto Blocker isn't without its complications, especially for users who like to sideload apps, work with developer tools or install software from outside the Google Play Store or the Samsung Galaxy Store. Epic Games even filed a lawsuit against Samsung a couple of years ago, arguing that this very feature made downloading third-party apps unnecessarily difficult. Understanding what Auto Blocker actually does and what it doesn't can help you make a smarter decision about whether to keep it on, turn it off or somewhere in between. Let's see what this feature does, how you can enable or disable it and what's the best thing to do. Auto Blocker is a built-in security feature available on Galaxy devices using One UI 6 or higher. Its main job is to stop app installation from outside the Google Play Store or Samsung's Galaxy Store, efficiently closing off one of the most common ways malware ends up on a phone. It also takes things a step further and blocks malicious commands sent through a USB cable, which matters if you've ever charged your phone using a public cable. Beyond that, Auto Blocker filters images suspected of containing malicious code in messaging apps like Samsung Messages, Google Messages, Messenger, WhatsApp or Telegram. For users who want even stronger protections, Samsung offers another mode called "Maximum restrictions," which adds extra safeguards, such as blocking device admin apps and work profiles, disabling 2G network connections, preventing auto-reconnection to unsecured Wi-Fi and stripping location data from shared photos. It's definitely a more aggressive setting, increasing security at the expense of convenience. Epic Games sued Google and Samsung back in 2024. The feature, they said, combined with existing Play Store and Galaxy Store flows, forced users to take over 20 steps just to download the Epic Games Store. The lawsuit was eventually dropped after Epic reached an agreement with Samsung , but the Auto Blocker stayed on. If you need to sideload an app or run a developer tool, you can turn Auto Blocker off by going to Settings > Security and privacy > Auto Blocker and tapping the toggle. You'll need to authenticate before switching it off, which is a great feature that can protect you if someone gets their hands on your phone and tries to install some malware. The same path lets you turn it back on. On phones running One UI 8.5 or later, you can also enable an option that automatically turns Auto Blocker back on 30 minutes after it's disabled. This lets you temporarily disable the protection to install an app without having to remember to reactivate it. You can find this extra toggle by tapping on the Auto Blocker feature in the menu. As you'd expect, Samsung recommends keeping Auto Blocker on, and for most users, that's sound advice. The feature is efficient in guarding against malicious apps, unauthorized USB access and tampered software updates; threats that are easy to overlook until something goes wrong. The trade-offs are real, though, because Auto Blocker intentionally blocks APK installs from outside the Play Store and Galaxy Store, which affects anyone who relies on open-source apps or sideloaded tools. The most balanced approach is to leave Auto Blocker enabled by default and disable it only when you have a specific reason to install something from outside official app stores. Once you're done, you turn it back on, or, if you're running One UI 8.5 or later, you can have it automatically turn back on after 30 minutes. If you're an advanced user who sideloads often, the auto re-enable option can feel like a nuisance. Just keep in mind that disabling Auto Blocker removes an additional layer of security. Other protections, including Google Play Protect , can still help guard against malicious apps, but it's important to verify the source of anything you install from outside official app stores. For people who want the opposite approach, Samsung's Maximum restrictions mode adds plenty of extra protections.

passages: Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content.

The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income.
Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs.
I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer.
Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs.

To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once.
Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious.

“I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board.

For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions.

Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

passages: Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year .

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations.
Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted.

Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device .
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone. The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device . The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush. Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights. For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things. All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates. To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them. In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.) With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free. Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more. The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering. All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app. The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter. With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.
